exp: In atrial fibrillation with WPW, AV-nodal blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, adenosine, beta-blockers) preferentially slow conduction through the AV node, paradoxically diverting and accelerating impulses down the accessory (Kent) bundle — this can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide, by contrast, slows conduction in the accessory pathway itself and is a preferred acute pharmacological option in this setting. Avoid IV amiodarone too: the 2019 AHA/ACC/HRS AF update rates it potentially harmful in pre-excited AF.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Grey baby syndrome in neonates receiving chloramphenicol is due to immaturity of which hepatic enzyme?
why: G6PD deficiency causes haemolysis with oxidant drugs, not grey baby syndrome
Correct: immature glucuronyl transferase stops chloramphenicol conjugation, so it accumulates
CYP3A4 is not the main clearance route of chloramphenicol
N-acetyltransferase acetylates drugs such as isoniazid, not chloramphenicol
exp: Neonates, especially preterm infants, have immature hepatic glucuronyl transferase and reduced renal clearance, so chloramphenicol accumulates to toxic levels. This produces grey baby syndrome - abdominal distension, vomiting, ashen-grey cyanosis, hypotension, and cardiovascular collapse - typically 2-9 days after starting therapy, which is why neonatal chloramphenicol dosing demands extreme caution and level monitoring.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Which enzyme degrades bradykinin, and whose inhibition explains the dry cough seen with ACE inhibitor therapy?
why: Kininase I is a plasma carboxypeptidase and a minor pathway; it is not blocked by ACE inhibitors
Correct: kininase II is ACE itself; its inhibition lets bradykinin build up and cause cough
Carboxypeptidase N is the plasma form of kininase I, a minor pathway unrelated to ACE inhibitor cough
Neutral endopeptidase (neprilysin) is the target of sacubitril, not of ACE inhibitors
exp: ACE is identical to kininase II, which normally degrades bradykinin alongside converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II; ACE inhibitors cause bradykinin accumulation, which is responsible for the characteristic dry, persistent cough and rarely angioedema, a class effect not shared by ARBs since they do not affect bradykinin metabolism.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Rapid intravenous infusion of vancomycin is classically associated with which non-allergic reaction caused by direct mast cell degranulation?
why: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a delayed T-cell mediated reaction, not rate related
Correct: rapid vancomycin infusion causes direct, non-IgE histamine release from mast cells
Serum sickness is a type III immune-complex reaction
Fixed drug eruption is a T-cell reaction that recurs at the same skin site
exp: Red man syndrome is a rate-related infusion reaction, not a true IgE-mediated allergy, caused by direct non-immune histamine release from mast cells when vancomycin is infused too fast; it presents with flushing, pruritus, and an erythematous rash over the face, neck, and upper torso, and is managed by slowing the infusion and antihistamine premedication, not by labelling the patient vancomycin-allergic.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Which class of antihypertensive is contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
why: Calcium channel blockers do not remove efferent arteriolar tone and are safe
Alpha blockers do not block angiotensin II at the efferent arteriole
Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar dilator that does not remove the angiotensin II support to GFR
Correct: ACE inhibitors remove angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction, collapsing GFR in bilateral stenosis
exp: In renal artery stenosis the glomerular filtration pressure depends on angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. Blocking it collapses the filtration gradient and precipitates acute kidney injury. ARBs share the contraindication.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Which electrolyte abnormality most characteristically precipitates digoxin toxicity?
why: Hyperkalaemia does not potentiate digoxin; it is a feature of acute massive overdose, not its trigger
Correct: low potassium leaves more Na-K-ATPase sites free for digoxin, causing toxicity even at therapeutic levels
Hypernatraemia has no recognised link to digoxin toxicity
Hyperchloraemia has no recognised link to digoxin toxicity
exp: Digoxin and potassium compete for the same binding site on Na-K-ATPase, so a low potassium leaves more digoxin bound and toxicity appears even at therapeutic levels. This matters because loop and thiazide diuretics are commonly co-prescribed.

subject: Pharmacology
q: A patient on antitubercular therapy reports declining vision with impaired red-green colour discrimination. Which drug is responsible?
why: Correct: ethambutol causes dose-dependent optic neuritis with loss of acuity and red-green discrimination
Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy, prevented with pyridoxine
Rifampicin causes hepatotoxicity, orange body fluids and a flu-like syndrome
Pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia
exp: Ethambutol causes dose-dependent retrobulbar optic neuritis with loss of acuity and red-green colour vision, which is why colour vision is documented before starting it. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (prevented with pyridoxine), not optic neuritis.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Histamine acting on which receptor mediates the wheal-and-flare (triple response of Lewis) in skin?
why: Correct — H1 mediates the vasodilation, increased permeability and axon-reflex flare/itch of the triple response.
H2 mediates gastric acid secretion, not the cutaneous flare response.
H3 is a presynaptic CNS autoreceptor regulating histamine release, unrelated to the skin response.
H4 is expressed on immune cells (eosinophils/mast cells) with a chemotactic role, not the classic triple response.
exp: The triple response of Lewis (localized red spot, flare, wheal) after intradermal histamine is mediated via H1 receptors on vascular endothelium and sensory nerve endings, distinct from H2-mediated gastric acid secretion, the target of H2 blockers like ranitidine.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Which antiarrhythmic drug class was shown to increase post-myocardial-infarction mortality in the CAST trial, despite effectively suppressing PVCs?
why: Amiodarone is actually preferred post-MI because of its low proarrhythmic risk relative to Class I agents.
Lidocaine is used for acute ventricular arrhythmia but was not the CAST-implicated class and lacks that long-term mortality signal.
Sotalol carries its own torsades risk but was not the class shown to increase mortality in CAST.
Correct — Class IC drugs (flecainide, encainide) increased mortality post-MI in the CAST trial, so they are avoided in structural/ischemic heart disease.
exp: The CAST trial showed Class IC antiarrhythmics (flecainide, encainide) suppress PVCs but increase mortality after MI due to proarrhythmia in structurally abnormal hearts — a classic example of a surrogate endpoint failing clinically, and a reason Class IC drugs are avoided in ischemic heart disease.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Initiating leuprolide (a GnRH agonist) in metastatic prostate cancer transiently worsens symptoms in the first 1-2 weeks due to which phenomenon?
opts: Initial gonadotropin surge (flare) before pituitary desensitization
Peripheral conversion to a more potent androgen
Loss of negative feedback on GnRH pulsatility
why: GnRH agonists do not block the androgen receptor directly — that is the role of antiandrogens like bicalutamide, added specifically to prevent the flare.
Correct — continuous GnRH agonist exposure transiently stimulates gonadotropins and testosterone before achieving chemical castration.
Peripheral conversion to a more potent androgen is not the mechanism of GnRH-agonist flare.
This describes the opposite of what actually happens with continuous GnRH agonism.
exp: GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin) cause an initial testosterone flare before achieving chemical castration through pituitary receptor downregulation — an antiandrogen is co-administered for the first 2-4 weeks in prostate cancer to blunt this flare, especially with bone metastases or cord-compression risk.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability) following antipsychotic use is treated with which drug that acts as a direct skeletal-muscle relaxant by blocking ryanodine-receptor calcium release?
why: Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) helps NMS but works centrally, not via ryanodine receptors.
Amantadine is also a dopaminergic adjunct in NMS, not a ryanodine-receptor blocker.
Benzodiazepines help agitation/rigidity symptomatically but do not act on ryanodine receptors.
Correct — dantrolene directly blocks sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release in skeletal muscle.
exp: Dantrolene is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant that blocks the ryanodine receptor to prevent calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum — used in both neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia, unlike bromocriptine/amantadine which work centrally on dopamine pathways.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Drugs Affecting Blood and Blood formation
q: Eltrombopag increases platelet count in chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura refractory to steroids/IVIG by acting as an agonist at which receptor?
why: GPIIb/IIIa is a platelet fibrinogen receptor, targeted by antagonists like abciximab/eptifibatide, unrelated to eltrombopag.
Correct — eltrombopag (oral) and romiplostim (subcutaneous) are TPO-receptor agonists boosting platelet production.
GPIb is the von Willebrand factor receptor on platelets, unrelated to eltrombopag's mechanism.
P2Y12 is the ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel, an antiplatelet target, not a production-stimulating one.
exp: Eltrombopag and romiplostim are thrombopoietin-receptor agonists that stimulate megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production, used in steroid/IVIG-refractory chronic ITP — a different strategy from splenectomy or immunosuppression, and distinct from antiplatelet drugs targeting GPIIb/IIIa or P2Y12.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Repeated doses of ephedrine given in quick succession show a progressively diminishing pressor response — this phenomenon is termed?
why: Correct — tachyphylaxis reflects rapid depletion of releasable noradrenaline stores with repeated indirect-acting sympathomimetic dosing.
Tolerance develops over days-to-weeks of repeated dosing (e.g., opioids, nitrates), not within minutes.
Idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal response, unrelated to repeated dosing.
Hypersensitivity is an immune-mediated allergic reaction, not a pharmacodynamic dosing phenomenon.
exp: Tachyphylaxis is the rapid, short-interval decline in response to repeated drug doses, classically demonstrated by indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine, tyramine) that deplete releasable noradrenaline stores from nerve terminals, distinguishing it from tolerance, which develops over a longer timescale.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Drug A produces its maximal analgesic effect at a lower dose than Drug B, though both achieve the same maximum effect. Drug A is said to have greater...?
why: Efficacy refers to the maximal effect achievable, which is stated to be equal between the two drugs.
Bioavailability concerns the fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation, not addressed by this comparison.
Correct — a lower effective dose for the same effect means greater potency.
Therapeutic index is the ratio of toxic to effective dose, not what is being compared here.
exp: Potency (dose needed for a given effect) and efficacy (maximum achievable effect) are independent dose-response properties — a more potent drug needs a lower dose, but potency says nothing about how effective the drug ultimately is, tested via leftward curve shifts (potency) versus curve height (efficacy).

subject: Pharmacology
q: Bedaquiline, used in multidrug-resistant tuberculosis regimens, acts by inhibiting which bacterial target?
why: DNA gyrase is inhibited by fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin/moxifloxacin), also used in MDR-TB but via a different mechanism.
Correct — bedaquiline blocks mycobacterial ATP synthase, causing ATP depletion.
RNA polymerase is the rifampicin target, not bedaquiline's.
The 30S ribosomal subunit is targeted by aminoglycosides/tetracyclines, unrelated to bedaquiline.
exp: Bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, starving the organism of energy — a mechanism distinct from the older first-line drugs. It carries a boxed QT-prolongation warning, so baseline and periodic ECGs are mandatory in MDR-TB regimens under NTEP.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Levosimendan improves cardiac contractility in acute decompensated heart failure primarily by which mechanism?
opts: Calcium-sensitization of troponin C without raising intracellular calcium
why: PDE3 inhibition (milrinone) raises cAMP and calcium influx — a different inotrope class from levosimendan.
Beta-1 agonism (dobutamine) increases contractility via a cAMP/calcium route, not calcium sensitization.
Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition is digoxin's mechanism, not levosimendan's.
Correct — levosimendan sensitizes troponin C to existing intracellular calcium rather than raising calcium levels.
exp: Levosimendan is a calcium sensitizer — it binds troponin C to enhance contractility at existing intracellular calcium levels, unlike PDE3 inhibitors (milrinone) or beta-agonists (dobutamine) which increase calcium influx. This lower oxygen-demand profile makes it useful in acute decompensated heart failure, though mortality-benefit evidence is mixed.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Which oral antidiabetic drug is best avoided in a patient with a past history of bladder cancer because of its association with an increased risk of recurrence?
why: Metformin has no bladder cancer association
Sulfonylureas are not linked to bladder cancer
Correct — pioglitazone is associated with increased bladder cancer risk
DPP-4 inhibitors carry no such association
exp: Pioglitazone, a PPAR-gamma agonist (thiazolidinedione), carries a recognized association with bladder cancer risk in addition to its known fluid retention/heart failure risk, and is avoided in patients with current or past bladder cancer.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Tazobactam, when combined with piperacillin, protects the antibiotic from bacterial resistance by which mechanism?
opts: Inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit
Chelating divalent cations required for peptidoglycan cross-linking
Irreversible (suicide) inhibition of bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes
why: Transpeptidase/PBP inhibition is piperacillin's own mechanism, not tazobactam's
30S inhibition describes aminoglycosides/tetracyclines
Not a recognized mechanism for tazobactam
Correct — irreversible beta-lactamase inhibition
exp: Beta-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam) have weak intrinsic antibacterial activity; they act by irreversibly binding and inactivating bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes, protecting the co-administered beta-lactam antibiotic from hydrolysis and extending its spectrum to beta-lactamase-producing organisms.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Drugs Affecting Blood and Blood formation
q: Which anticoagulant selectively and indirectly inhibits factor Xa via antithrombin III binding, has no direct action on thrombin, and is considered safe in a patient with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
why: Correct — indirect, selective factor Xa inhibition via antithrombin, HIT-safe
Unfractionated heparin is the classic HIT trigger
Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, not indirect factor Xa inhibitor
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, unrelated to antithrombin/factor Xa binding
exp: Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide that binds antithrombin III to selectively accelerate factor Xa inhibition, without direct thrombin activity and without binding platelet factor 4, making it a preferred parenteral anticoagulant in patients with a history of HIT.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Hydrochlorothiazide reduces urinary calcium excretion, an effect used to prevent recurrent calcium renal stones. What does it do to serum calcium, and by what mechanism?
opts: Hypocalcemia via increased urinary calcium excretion
Hypercalcemia via enhanced distal tubular calcium reabsorption
No significant effect on calcium handling
Hypercalcemia via suppression of parathyroid hormone
why: Describes loop diuretics (furosemide), the opposite effect
Correct — enhanced distal tubular calcium reabsorption
Thiazides do have a clinically significant calcium-conserving effect
The mechanism is tubular, not via PTH suppression
exp: Unlike loop diuretics (which increase urinary calcium excretion via NKCC2 inhibition), thiazides inhibit the distal NCC transporter, which secondarily enhances distal tubular calcium reabsorption, reducing urinary calcium excretion — used therapeutically to reduce calcium-stone recurrence in idiopathic hypercalciuria.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Enalapril requires hepatic hydrolysis to its active metabolite (enalaprilat) before it can exert its antihypertensive effect. Which pharmacological term describes this property?
why: Partial agonist relates to submaximal receptor efficacy, unrelated to metabolic activation
Inverse agonist produces the opposite effect at a constitutively active receptor
Correct — prodrug requires biotransformation to the active form
Allosteric modulator acts at a site distinct from the orthosteric site
exp: A prodrug is a pharmacologically inactive or less active compound converted in vivo, commonly by hepatic metabolism, to the active drug. Enalapril to enalaprilat is a classic example, alongside prednisone to prednisolone and levodopa to dopamine.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) converts angiotensin II into which peptide, which then acts via the Mas receptor to produce vasodilatory and anti-proliferative effects opposing the classical renin-angiotensin system?
why: Angiotensin III comes from aminopeptidase action on angiotensin II and retains pressor activity
Bradykinin is degraded by ACE, unrelated to the ACE2 pathway
Angiotensin I is the ACE substrate upstream of angiotensin II
Correct — angiotensin (1-7) acting via the Mas receptor
exp: The ACE2-angiotensin (1-7)-Mas receptor axis is a counter-regulatory arm of the renin-angiotensin system, opposing the vasoconstrictive, proliferative, and pro-fibrotic effects of the classical ACE-angiotensin II-AT1 axis; ACE2 is also the cellular entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Which beta-blocker has an ultra-short elimination half-life of approximately 9 minutes due to rapid hydrolysis by red blood cell esterases, making it suited for titratable perioperative heart-rate control?
why: Correct — esterase-hydrolyzed, ultra-short half-life
Metoprolol is hepatically (CYP2D6) metabolized with a half-life of hours
Propranolol is hepatically metabolized, half-life of hours
Atenolol is renally eliminated, half-life about 6-9 hours
exp: Esmolol is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma/RBC esterases rather than the liver, giving an approximately 9-minute half-life that allows rapid titration and offset, useful for perioperative tachycardia/hypertension and acute rate control in SVT.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Mesna is co-administered with cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide chemotherapy specifically to prevent which toxicity?
why: Cardiotoxicity is an anthracycline (doxorubicin) concern
Correct — mesna neutralizes acrolein, preventing hemorrhagic cystitis
Peripheral neuropathy relates to vincristine/taxanes/platinum agents
Pulmonary fibrosis is a bleomycin toxicity
exp: Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are metabolized to acrolein, a urotoxic metabolite causing hemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna's free thiol group binds and inactivates acrolein in the urinary tract, and is co-administered with adequate hydration to prevent this toxicity without affecting antitumor activity.

subject: Pharmacology
q: Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole) achieves synergistic bactericidal activity through which mechanism?
opts: Both components inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase
Sequential blockade of two consecutive steps in bacterial folate synthesis
Combined inhibition of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits
why: Only trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; sulfamethoxazole acts at an earlier step
Neither component inhibits DNA gyrase, the fluoroquinolone mechanism
Correct — sequential folate-pathway blockade
Ribosomal inhibition describes aminoglycosides/macrolides, not co-trimoxazole
exp: Co-trimoxazole's synergy comes from sequential inhibition of bacterial folate synthesis: sulfamethoxazole blocks dihydropteroate synthase (competing with PABA), and trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase downstream, converting a bacteriostatic combination into a bactericidal one and reducing resistance emergence versus either drug alone.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Drugs Affecting Blood and Blood formation
q: Deficiency of which haematinic vitamin causes megaloblastic anaemia accompanied by subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, a neurological feature not seen with isolated folate deficiency?
why: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia but not cord degeneration
Pyridoxine deficiency causes sideroblastic anaemia/peripheral neuropathy, not this picture
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy
Correct — B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia plus subacute combined degeneration
exp: Both folate and B12 deficiency impair methionine synthase-mediated DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic anaemia, but B12 is uniquely also a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; its deficiency causes methylmalonic acid accumulation implicated in subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, which is specific to B12 deficiency and can be masked (anaemia-wise) but not prevented (neurologically) by folic acid alone.
